job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here are the issues I found, in section order, followed by a short note on which matter most. This is a text-only review. Counsel should confirm points that depend on existing law, especially how the bill interacts with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA).

**Sec. 2 (Definitions)**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, not per operator, affiliate group, or project. An operator could split recovery across several vessels, or across a collector vessel and shuttle or support vessels, and stay under the line on paper.
2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and tonnage.** "Recovery" is undefined: it could mean collection on the seafloor, lifting to the surface, or offloading. The bill also doesn't say whether tons are wet or dry (nodules carry substantial moisture), what period counts as a "year," or how tonnage is measured and verified.
3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and the 200-meter depth.** The language is not limited to nodules and arguably reaches oil and gas, sulfides, crusts, and dredging on the continental shelf. This creates overbreadth and conflicts with other regimes (e.g., OCS Lands Act leasing), and it could pull in other industries as opponents. The bill also doesn't say how depth is measured or whether it applies inside U.S. waters.
4. **Sec. 2(1)(B), Secretary's determination.** "Secretary" is undefined (Commerce? Interior?), and "risks... comparable to" has no standard, process, notice, or review. Because Sec. 5(b) attaches criminal penalties, this invites vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges.
5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), timing of determinations.** The bill doesn't say whether a determination applies prospectively only, when it takes effect, or whether it must be published. A company could face liability for activity that was lawful when conducted.
6. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and "corporations organized under the laws of a State." It omits foreign-incorporated subsidiaries, LLCs and partnerships (arguably), trusts, joint ventures, territorial or D.C. entities, and permanent residents. It has no ownership or control test, so restructuring through a foreign subsidiary is an obvious route.
7. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less escape the registry entirely, and the threshold doesn't match the 10,000-ton recovery test in Sec. 2(1)(A). "Equipped for the recovery" is vague, and the bill doesn't say which tonnage convention applies.
8. **Sec. 2, missing definitions.** "Person," "operator," "United States," "exploration license," "environmental assessment," "serious harm," and "deep-sea ecosystems" are all undefined. Each is a point of ambiguity litigants can use.

**Sec. 3 (Prohibition)**

9. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States."** Mining occurs at sea, and the bill doesn't say whether "United States" includes the EEZ, the OCS, or only the territorial sea. A foreign-owned or foreign-operated vessel on the high seas is outside the prohibition. Remote direction from a U.S. office is arguable at best.
10. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in."** The bill doesn't reach financing, offtake, processing, importing, or owning minerals recovered abroad. A company can shift to supply-chain roles or to non-U.S. partners.
11. **Sec. 3(a), extraterritorial reach.** Applying the prohibition to U.S. persons "anywhere" invites international-law and comity objections, and it is hard to enforce against conduct abroad. The bill has no findings or stated constitutional basis to support it.
12. **Sec. 3(b), grandfathering of "mining conducted under an exploration license."** This is likely the largest hole. It exempts mining under any exploration license issued before enactment, with no volume cap, duration, or limit on area, renewal, transfer, or successor. DSHMRA exploration licenses don't ordinarily authorize commercial recovery, so the text is confusing at best.
13. **Sec. 3(b), unspecified licensor.** "An exploration license" doesn't say who issued it. Read literally, it could include licenses or contracts from foreign states or the ISA, and the bill doesn't address licenses that are later modified, extended, or revoked.
14. **Sec. 3(b), incentive and timing.** The cutoff is the date of enactment, and enactment is followed by a 180-day gap before the Act takes effect (see Sec. 8). That creates a race to obtain licenses before enactment and invites disputes over pending applications and vested rights.
15. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** The test is "purpose," with no cap on volume, area, duration, or equipment. It requires no permit, reporting, or independent oversight, and it doesn't address mixed-purpose activity. It could cover bulk sampling or full-scale test mining.
16. **Interaction with existing law.** The bill neither amends nor repeals DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. ch. 26) or other seabed authorities. Existing license and permit regimes would conflict with the new prohibition, and the bill gives no rule on which controls. That is a strong basis for challenge and an enforcement problem.

**Sec. 4 (Registry)**

17. **Sec. 4(a), registration.** There is no deadline, no fee, no content requirements, and no rulemaking authority for NOAA. "Operator" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say how it applies to foreign-flag vessels or non-U.S. operators.
18. **Sec. 4(b), reports.** Report contents are unspecified (location, depth, tonnage, destination), and there are no audit, inspection, data-retention, or public-disclosure provisions. "Certified by the operator" is self-attestation, and the bill has no express false-certification penalty.
19. **Sec. 4, no penalty for noncompliance.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report has no stated consequence. A vessel that never registers submits nothing and is invisible to enforcers.
20. **Sec. 4, no verification tools.** The bill has no vessel tracking (e.g., AIS), onboard observers, or boarding authority. Proving tonnage recovered at depth would be hard.

**Sec. 5 (Penalties)**

21. **Sec. 5(a), retroactivity conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later (Sec. 8). That ambiguity is a fair-notice and due-process target.
22. **Sec. 5(a), "each day."** Because the prohibition turns on an annual tonnage threshold, it's unclear which days count as violation days. Is it every day after the threshold is crossed, or the whole year?
23. **Sec. 5(a), no assessment mechanism.** The bill doesn't say who assesses the civil penalty, what hearing rights apply, or whether DOJ must sue. It has no inflation adjustment, and at $1,000,000 per day it invites an Excessive Fines Clause challenge.
24. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully."** The mens rea standard is undefined (knowledge of the facts or of the law?). Combined with the Secretary's open-ended determination in Sec. 2(1)(B), it raises vagueness issues and gives defendants a strong defense.
25. **Sec. 5, no enforcement architecture.** The bill designates no enforcing agency and gives no investigative, search, seizure, or forfeiture authority. It has no in rem vessel liability, injunctive relief, officer or parent-company liability, conspiracy or attempt provisions, or venue and jurisdiction rules for conduct abroad.

**Sec. 6 (International agreement)**

26. **Sec. 6, "shall seek to negotiate."** This is hortatory. It has no consequence for failure, no reporting to Congress, and no definition of "equivalent prohibitions." It also doesn't address the U.S. position relative to UNCLOS and the ISA, so the provision is unenforceable.

**Sec. 7 (Duration)**

27. **Sec. 7(a), joint resolution mechanism.** A joint resolution must pass both chambers and be signed by the President (or survive a veto), so it is no easier than passing a law. The bill has no expedited procedure, no deadline or funding for the NASEM report, and no binding link between the report and the finding.
28. **Sec. 7(a), "serious harm."** The standard is undefined, and the bill doesn't say what follows a finding. It is unclear whether the finding itself lifts the prohibition or whether further legislation or a licensing framework is needed.
29. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), internal conflict.** Subsection (a) implies the prohibition lasts until Congress acts, while subsection (b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment regardless. This ambiguity affects planning and any challenge to the bill's intent.
30. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** When the Act "ceases to have effect," the bill doesn't say whether pending enforcement actions or penalties for earlier violations survive. Defendants could argue they don't.

**Sec. 8 (Effective date) and structural gaps**

31. **Sec. 8, 180-day gap.** Companies can ramp up operations between enactment and effective date, build reliance interests for takings or estoppel arguments, and rush toward grandfathering under Sec. 3(b).
32. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes Sec. 2(1)(B), the extraterritorial reach, or the retroactive penalty, the bill doesn't say whether the rest survives.
33. **No findings, jurisdictional basis, or judicial review provision.** The bill doesn't state its constitutional basis (Commerce Clause, treaty power) or the factual predicate for the prohibition. That makes it easier to challenge, and it leaves the Secretary's determinations without a specified review path.

**Where I'd focus before Thursday:**
- **Sec. 3(b), 3(c), and the DSHMRA interaction (12, 13, 15, 16).** These most directly determine whether companies keep operating.
- **Sec. 2(1)(B) with Sec. 5(b) (4, 5, 24).** This is the strongest legal-challenge argument.
- **Sec. 5(a) with Sec. 8 (21, 31).** The retroactivity mismatch is concrete and easy to explain to staff.
- **Sec. 2(1)(A) and the oil and gas overbreadth (3).** This could help build a broader coalition.

One caution: several of these cut both ways. Gaps in the registry and enforcement provisions (17 to 20, 25) matter to us only if the bill passes in roughly this form. If we raise them, sponsors may fix them, so decide which to hold for floor or litigation and which to raise at markup. I can turn these into talking points, a memo for member offices, or amendment language if useful.
